entities.summary:
A legal identification of a person in international law, establishing the person as a subject, a national, of a sovereign state.

This concept has its roots in ancient civilizations, with the concept of 'citizenship' emerging in ancient Greece and Rome. The modern concept of nationality as we know it today, however, is a product of the Enlightenment and the emergence of modern nation-states in Europe during the 17th and 18th centuries. The Treaty of Westphalia (1648) marked a significant turning point in the development of nationality, as it established the principle of sovereignty and the idea that states have the right to govern their own citizens.

The concept of nationality has had a profound impact on international law and diplomacy, shaping the way states interact with one another and define their relationships with their citizens. The idea of nationality has also been influential in the development of human rights and the concept of citizenship, with many international agreements and conventions based on the principle of nationality.

The legacy of nationality can be seen in modern nation-states, with many countries continuing to define themselves by their nationality and the rights and responsibilities that come with it. The concept of nationality has also been the subject of ongoing debate and discussion, with many scholars and thinkers questioning the relevance and validity of the concept in the modern world.

The significance of nationality lies in its ability to shape our understanding of identity, community, and belonging. It has the power to unite people across borders and create a sense of shared identity and purpose. At the same time, it has also been used to justify exclusion, discrimination, and violence against certain groups of people.
